title: Count a bin of hex nuts on a desk tally counter
instruction: Move the hex nuts from the bin into the empty tray, counting them on the tally counter.
context: Stock clerks doing cycle counts, receiving inspectors and lab technicians click a tally counter once for each item as they move it, so the count survives an interruption and is read off the counter at the end. The desk counter on the bench still shows the last count; a count starts from 0000. Done by: stock clerks, warehouse and receiving staff, lab technicians. This tests keeping a mechanical record in step with a physical transfer, with one hand moving parts and the other working a sprung key and a reset knob: a skipped step, a missed or doubled click or a dropped part leaves a plausible but wrong number.
setup: Positions are on the table top, measured forward from the line through the two arm bases and left (+) or right (-) of the midline between them; the arm bases are 610 mm apart. Nothing else is on the table. 1) Tally counter: a desk tally counter matching the Redington Model 18 desk tally (13-1804) in size and controls: chrome-plated steel case on a black ABS base plate (57 mm across, 5 mm thick), bolted to the table with the base centre 240 mm forward and 120 mm right; 66.5 mm tall overall. Its round case (46 mm across, 29.6 mm deep) has a 28 x 7 mm window facing the robot with four figure wheels (white 4 x 2.3 mm figures on black drums, 7 mm apart); it shows 0038. On top is a 10 mm round push key with a 7 mm stroke; one full stroke adds 1. On the case's right side is a reset knob, 13 mm across, standing 20 mm out from the case on a horizontal axis 31 mm above the table; turning its top away from the robot by 55 to 70 degrees returns the units and tens wheels to 0, and a spring returns the knob. The maker publishes neither key travel nor reset turn: here the key counts once pushed past 4.25 mm (about 2.5 N), and one 55 to 70 degree twist zeroes the count where the Redington knob is turned until all wheels read 0 (up to a full turn). The README gives every part, spring and size needed to build this counter. 2) Bin: a blue polypropylene parts tray, 163 mm front to back, 171 mm wide, 33 mm tall, 3 mm walls and floor, fixed with its centre 262 mm forward and 225 mm left. 3) Tray: a white polypropylene tray of the same build with 25 mm walls, fixed and empty, centre 98 mm forward and 115 mm left. 4) Eleven DIN 934 M16 hex nuts, zinc-plated steel, 24 mm across flats, 27.7 mm across corners, 13 mm thick, 16 mm bore, 33.3 g each, lying flat in the bin with two corners pointing forward, on a grid of four columns at 208, 244, 280 and 316 mm forward and three rows at 273, 225 and 177 mm left; the slot at 280 mm forward, 225 mm left is empty. The README lists every collider, joint, spring and mass of the counter.
scoring: A nut is over the tray when its centre is inside the tray's inner wall rectangle (157 x 165 mm) and between 3 mm (the floor top) and 50 mm above the table. N is the number of nuts over the tray that rest there: the nut's lowest point within 2 mm below to 3 mm above the floor top, or its centre above the outline of a nut already in N with its lowest point between that nut's mid-height and 3 mm above that nut's top. Nuts flat, on edge, touching a wall or stacked count; a nut on the wall top does not, and a nut still held over the tray with nothing under it does not (a held nut resting on the floor or on a counted nut does count toward N, but full credit needs it released). No credit unless the latched reading has been 0000 at some moment of the trial: a count that never shows a steady 0000 (carried on from 0038, or a reset twist too short to bring both wheels to 0) scores 0. The counter shows a valid reading only while the units and tens wheels are both within 6 degrees of a figure. The latched reading is the last valid reading the wheels showed for 0.25 s; it starts at the counter's 0038. Dropped: a nut centre outside both trays' outer footprints and less than 20 mm above the table, or more than 20 mm below the table top anywhere. Dropped is sticky: once it happens the score is 0 for the rest of the trial. Apart from the 0000 at some moment and the dropped rule, only the end state is graded: the order of clicks and placements (clicking before or after each nut, moving several nuts and then clicking for them, clicking ahead, or zeroing again mid-count and recounting) does not change the score. Released: every gripper TCP at least 30 mm from each nut's bounding box and from the bounding boxes of the key and the reset knob. At rest, over the last 1 s: each nut within 1 mm and 2 degrees of its current pose and slower than 1 cm/s; both wheels within 2 degrees of a figure and each varying by at most 0.3 degrees; the key within 0.5 mm of its top stop and varying by at most 0.2 mm; the knob within 2 degrees of its rest stop. With no nut dropped: 1.0 = all 11 nuts in the tray, latched reading 11, the wheels showing 0011 now, released and at rest. 0.8 = all 11 in the tray and latched reading 11, but not released, not at rest or the wheels between figures now. 0.25 = all 11 in the tray and latched reading 10 or 12 (one missed or one extra click, whichever order the robot clicks and places in). 0.4 x N / 11, rounded to 3 decimals = 1 <= N <= 10 and latched reading N (an accurate but unfinished count). 0 otherwise: the untouched start, no steady 0000 at any moment, a dropped nut, all 11 in the tray with a reading off by 2 or more, or a partial count with a reading other than N. Success is 1.0 held for 1 s.
reset_notes: Use zero object jitter. Restore the eleven nuts flat in their bin slots with the same slot empty, the tray empty, the counter's wheels on 0038, the key up and the knob on its rest stop (the spring holds it at -1 degree). Nothing is consumed. The scorer's latched reading (38), its remembered 0000 and dropped flags and its 1 s windows start fresh with each trial.
fidelity: The counter's internals (pawl, detents, carry, heart-cam reset) are our design after a 1951 patent; key stroke and spring forces are estimates. Only the units and tens wheels turn. Figures are 7 mm apart (real: 5 mm) and the knob stands 20 mm out (real: 8 mm) so the pads can pinch it. Presses count at key speeds up to 150 mm/s. The counter is bolted down. Friction is 1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic. Full list in the README.
